subject: business-studies

moments.title: How Competitive Forces Shape Strategy
moments.body: Porter's Harvard Business Review article introduces the five forces framework: rivalry, buyer power, supplier power, threat of entry, threat of substitutes. The article is one of HBR's most-reprinted.
moments.takeaway: Strategy is reframed from competitor-by-competitor analysis to industry-structure analysis.

moments.title: Competitive Strategy
moments.body: Porter's book extends the five forces framework and introduces three generic strategies: cost leadership, differentiation, focus. The book becomes the most-cited strategy text of the 1980s and 1990s.
moments.takeaway: Strategy becomes a discipline with explicit frameworks, taught in MBA programmes worldwide.

moments.title: Competitive Advantage
moments.body: The follow-up introduces the value chain — disaggregating a firm into primary and support activities to identify where competitive advantage can be built.
moments.takeaway: Internal analysis joins external analysis in Porter's framework.

now.title: Porter today
now.body: Five forces is still the most-taught industry framework in business education. Critics (W. Chan Kim and Renee Mauborgne's 'Blue Ocean Strategy', 2005) argue Porter underweights innovation in creating new markets rather than competing in existing ones. Platform economics and network effects complicate the original framework.
now.open_questions: How do five forces apply to multi-sided platforms (Uber, Airbnb) where the 'buyer' and 'supplier' distinction is fuzzy?

reflection: Porter's frameworks were criticised in the 2000s as too static; they have outlived most of the critiques.
